messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 72
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Coast Guard
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 76

# Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his hands folded in his lap, the afternoon light catching the silver in his hair. At seventy-two, he carries himself with the disciplined posture of someone who spent forty-three years in the Coast Guard, though lately his shoulders seem to curve inward, as if he's trying to make himself smaller.

He was stationed in Port-au-Prince in 1998 when a cargo ship caught fire in the harbor. Marcus was a senior officer then, forty-seven years old, at the height of his career. The vessel was transporting industrial solvents and pesticides destined for agricultural distribution across the Caribbean. When the fire broke out in the hold, the crew couldn't contain it. Marcus and his team responded immediately—this was what they trained for, what they'd done dozens of times before.

What they didn't know was the extent of the chemical load or how the fire would transform those compounds into something far more dangerous. As Marcus directed rescue operations from the deck, thick clouds of toxic vapor rolled across the water. He remembers the smell first—acrid, chemical, nothing like anything he'd encountered before. Then came the burning in his eyes, his throat, his lungs. His team was coughing, some collapsed. Marcus kept working. He was the commanding officer. You don't leave your post.

By the time they evacuated, Marcus had inhaled substantial quantities of the fumes. He spent two weeks in a Port-au-Prince hospital, his lungs inflamed, his vision blurred from chemical burns. The doctors said he was lucky. He would recover. He did—physically. His lungs cleared. His vision returned. He was cleared to return to duty.

But something shifted that day, something invisible that no medical scan could capture.

For the first few years after, Marcus functioned. He completed his remaining years of service, retired with honors, and settled into civilian life with his wife, Yvonne. They had plans—travel, grandchildren's graduations, the slow pleasure of growing old together. Yet Marcus found himself increasingly trapped in a different kind of fog.

Now, at seventy-two, Marcus hasn't been able to sleep through the night in over two decades. He wakes at 3 a.m., gasping, convinced he's back on that burning ship, that chemical taste coating his mouth. During the day, unexpected smells trigger him—a neighbor's lawn treatment, someone's cleaning products at the grocery store—and suddenly his heart is racing, his chest is tight, and he's convinced he's suffocating again. Yvonne will find him standing in the kitchen, gripping the counter, unable to explain what's wrong.

He's become hypervigilant about air quality, insisting on expensive filtration systems for their home. He avoids going out when the air quality index is elevated. He won't visit his daughter in the city because of traffic pollution. What started as reasonable caution has narrowed his world considerably.

The worst part, Marcus says quietly, is the guilt. His crew members got sick too, some far worse than him. One man developed respiratory disease that eventually killed him at fifty-nine. Marcus wonders why he survived relatively intact while others suffered lasting damage. He carries the weight of that inequity every day, though he's never fully articulated it to anyone until now.

Yvonne sits beside him during this session. She's patient but tired. She wants her husband back—not the man from before the fire, but the man who can enjoy a sunset without analyzing the air quality, who can hold his grandchildren without worrying about invisible hazards, who can sleep beside her without waking in terror.

Marcus looks at his hands and says he doesn't know how to be anything other than what he is now.
